units.text: Materials and methods

All chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, Fisher Scientific, A2B Chem, Ambeed, Combi Blocks Inc., Enamine Ltd. or TCI Chemicals and were used as received.All solvents were of at least reagent grade, and dry/anoxic reactions were performed with solvents obtained from a solvent purification system, except for DMF, which was stirred with calcium hydride, filtered, then distilled onto 4Å molecular sieves under nitrogen.TTM, 1,2 HMT, 3,4 Pyrr3HMT BF4 5 and 1,2,3,4,5-pentachloro-6-(dichloromethyl)benzene 6 were prepared according to literature procedures.

Single crystal X-ray diffraction was performed using a Bruker D8 Venture diffractometer.Mass spectrometry was performed in positive mode on a Bruker Maxis Impact LC-MS Q-TOF instrument. 1 H NMR and 13 C NMR spectra were collected on a Varian 500 MHz NMR or Bruker AVIIIHD 800 MHz NMR spectrometer at 20 o C, unless otherwise specified.Electron spin resonance spectra were obtained with a Bruker Elexsys E580 X-band EPR spectrometer.-g-factors for the radicals were determined by measuring radicals in DCM solution compared to TTM in DCM solution as a standard. 2,7All radicals' spectra were collected within ~25 minutes of collecting the standard sample.The error margin for g factors was determined by taking two different samples of the same radical (TTM) in DCM and remeasuring them 3 times each over a 30 min span.The difference in calculated g factor changed by 0.00009 over the course of the 30 minutes.

Electrochemistry experiments were performed at room temperature in argon purged 0.2 M Bu4PF6 solution with ca.0.5 mg/mL analyte, in freshly distilled DCM using a Pt disc as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl wire as a reference electrode, and Pt wire as the counter electrode, at 100 mV scan rate, unless otherwise specified.These experiments used a CH Instruments 760C Potentiostat and BASi C-3 Cell Stand and the electrodes were polished using alumina paste on a polishing pad.Ferrocene's oxidation (Fc/Fc+) was used as an internal reference unless otherwise noted.Spectra are plotted according to IUPAC convention.UV-Vis spectra were collected on a JASCO V670 spectrometer in quartz cuvettes.Luminescence measurements were performed on a Horiba Fluorolog 3 fluorometer.

Photodecomposition experiments were performed in HPLC grade chlorobenzene dried over activated 4 Å molecular sieves for 24 h.The solutions were prepared by placing each radical in its own half-dram glass vial with a vinyl cap then 2 mL of the chlorobenzene were added for a final concentration of ca. 1 mM.The vials were evenly placed in a 4 cm diameter circle around the centre of a rotating stage, set 50 cm from a Kessil LED 370 nm lamp (40 W), and rotated at a speed of 0.5 rpm during the course of illumination.During the course of the experiment, UV spectra were collected by ceasing irradiation and using precision glass syringes to withdraw 50 uL of analyte solution, which was then diluted with 0.6 mL of dichloromethane in a quartz cuvette.Background spectra were collected before each time point.Relative peak intensity compared to t = 0 at the d0 → d1 λmax were plotted over time.

DFT, MP2, HF and CCSD calculations were performed using Gaussian 16. 8 CCSD energy calculations were performed using B3LYP optimized geometries and the 3-21G* basis set.Unless otherwise noted, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the B3LYP hybrid functional and 6-31G(d) basis set.Time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) calculations were performed for the first excited state and natural transition orbitals were generated for the first transition.To calculate the energy of PTM's and HMT's conformation in the crystal phase, the molecular coordinates of a single molecule were extracted from the crystal structure data, the dihedral angles between the aryl rings and the plane of the radical core were frozen, and an optimization was performed in the gas phase.Reorganization energy is calculated as the difference between the TD-DFT electronic energy of the geometry of the ground state (at the first excited state) and the optimized geometry of the first excited state.Bond dissociation energy (BDE) is calculated as the adduct's electronic energy (peroxy radical or peroxide dimer) minus the sum of the energies of the individual molecules (for the peroxy radical, triplet oxygen and the radical; for the peroxide dimer, two separate radicals and triplet oxygen).Free energy incorporates the thermal correction factors for radical, peroxy-radical and oxygen.Calculations performed in the gas phase.
Synthesis of CMT radicals and their precursors

We first attempted to react 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene with undecachlorodiphenylmethane similar to the classic procedure to synthesize PTMs. 1 We screened a variety of catalysts (including TiCl4, SnCl4, triflic acid) but these attempts failed, generally giving a complex mixture of products, possibly due to the cleavage of the methoxy groups or the relatively low reactivity of the benzyl chloride.Therefore, we envisioned a milder route from pentachlorobenzaldehyde or decachlorobenzhydrol, the latter of which was prepared by lithiation of hexachlorobenzene with BuLi followed by its double addition onto ethyl formate, affording a poorly soluble powder that could be purified simply by trituration with ethyl acetate and water.Careful control of this reaction's stoichiometry was important, as excess of either reagent (Ar-Li or ethyl formate) led to poor yields.

With these building blocks in hand we next explored Friedel-Crafts alkylation conditions.For pentachlorobenzaldehyde, Lewis acid catalysis at elevated temperature proved effective, using scandium triflate in nitromethane.Conversely, for the decachlorobenzhydrol, condensation proceeded with a Brønsted acid, in neat triflic acid.The reactions with 1-chloro-3,5-dimethoxybenzene showed a moderate preference for the alkylation of the C2 position, probably due to the larger size (A value) of methoxy compared to chlorine.These reactions afforded the triarylmethanes CM6T-H, CM4T-H, CM3T-H and CM2T-H.

The synthesis of the radicals was first attempted by deprotonating the triarylmethanes with a hydroxide base like Bu4NOH(aq) or KOH in THF to afford the anion, then an oxidant like p-chloranil or DDQ, as is typically 2,9 used for TTM/PTM to afford the radical.Most of the triarylmethanes were poorly soluble in THF, but in other solvents (DCM, DMF, DMSO), use of Bu4NOH(aq) seemed to lead to formation of a significant amount of side products.One possible issue could be due to the presence of water.HRMS analysis of one of the main side products showed formation of a phenolic trityl, presumably due to nucleophilic attack at the para position of one of the aryl rings, displacing a chloride.Instead, we switched to excess NaH in DMF with gentle heating followed by air as a mild oxidant, which afforded the desired products.Deprotonation of the more electron-rich CM3T-H took longer than CM2T-H.

Pentachlorobenzaldehyde. 1,2,3,4,5-pentachloro-6-(dichloromethyl)benzene 6 (988 mg, 2.97 mmol) and a stir bar were added to a three-necked round-bottom flask equipped with a reflux condenser.The flask was sealed with septa, evacuated and backfilled with nitrogen thrice, then oleum (20%, 9 mL) was added and the mixture was stirred at 95 °C.After 2 hours, the reaction was removed from heat and allowed to reach room temperature.Ice was slowly added to the reaction mixture before pouring it into 50 mL deionized water.The resulting greyish-white precipitate was filtered off and purified by filtration through silica (ca.200 g) using 5:1 hexanes:ethyl acetate to afford a tan solid of pure product (808 mg, 98%). 1 H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 10.34 (s, 1 H).Spectrum matches that reported in the literature.Decachlorobenzhydrol. Hexachlorobenzene (2.51 g, 8.8 mmol) was placed in a flame-dried 100 mL round bottom flask with a stir bar and sealed with a septum.The flask was evacuated and backfilled with nitrogen three times, then dry diethyl ether (35 mL) was added to the flask.The flask was placed in an acetone/dry ice bath that was maintained at -25 °C and the suspension was stirred at this temperature for a few minutes to ensure the temperature had equilibrated.Then, n-butyllithium (3.50 mL, 8.8 mmol, 2.5 M in hexanes) was added dropwise and reaction stirred for about 5 minutes.The generation of the aryllithium intermediate could be tracked visually by the dissolution of hexachlorobenzene to form a clear golden, or sometimes clear brownish, solution.Next, the flask was cooled to -78 °C and allowed to stir for another few minutes to allow for temperature equilibration.To this flask was added ethyl formate (0.35 mL, d = 0.917 g/mL, 4.4 mmol) dropwise.The flask was allowed to slowly warm to room temperature and stirred for 16 h.The reaction was quenched by adding methanol (15 mL) and concentrated in vacuo to afford a yellow chalky solid.Ethyl acetate (20 mL) and deionized water (20 mL) were added to the flask and the solid was vigorously homogenized while scratching the precipitate off the walls of the flask.The mixture was filtered and the solid rinsed with another portion of ethyl acetate (20 mL), affording an off-white solid (1.40 g, 59%).CM3T-H.Decachlorobenzhydrol (300 mg, 0.57 mmol) and 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene (1.00 g, 5.9 mmol) were combined in an oven-dried 25 mL round bottom flask with a stir bar.The flask was sealed with a septum, then evacuated and backfilled with nitrogen thrice.The flask was placed in an ice bath, then triflic acid (1.9 mL) was added dropwise.The mixture was allowed to stir for 20 min, then it was placed in an oil bath at 80 °C and stirred for 16 hours.The flask was removed from the oil bath and allowed to reach room temperature before pouring into a separatory funnel containing 50 mL each distilled water and dichloromethane.The DCM was drained off and the aqueous layer was extracted again with 50 mL DCM.The combined organic extracts were dried with magnesium sulfate, filtered and concentrated in vacuo to afford an orange-brown oil.This oil was purified by flash chromatography using a 5:1 hexanes:chloroform eluent to afford a white solid of pure CM3T-H (135 mg, 35%).(Note: If the desired product from the column is contaminated with 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene, trituration with ~40 mL hot ethyl acetate followed by filtration affords a pure product.) 1 H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 6.75 (s, 1 H), 6.11 (s, 1 H), 6.02 (s, 1 H), 3.82 (s, 3 H), 3.73 (s, 3 H), 3.45 (s, 3 H).(Note: the hindered rotation around the CH-Ar bond renders the two methoxy groups chemically inequivalent.This is also observed for the aryl protons in TTM-H.CM2T-H.Decachlorobenzhydrol (100 mg, 0.19 mmol) and 1-chloro-3,5-trimethoxybenzene (400 mg, 2.3 mmol) were combined in an oven-dried 25 mL round bottom flask with a stir bar.The flask was sealed with a septum, then evacuated and backfilled with nitrogen thrice.The flask was placed in an ice bath, then triflic acid (0.6 mL) was added dropwise.The mixture was stirred for 20 min, then it was placed in an oil bath at 75 °C and stirred for 16 hours.The flask was removed from the oil bath and allowed to reach room temperature before pouring into a separatory funnel containing 50 mL each distilled water and dichloromethane.The DCM was drained off, then the aqueous layer was extracted again with 50 mL DCM.The combined organic phases were dried with magnesium sulfate then filtered and concentrated in vacuo to afford an orange-brown oil, which was purified by flash chromatography using a gradient of hexanes:chloroform eluent (10:1 to 8:1), affording a white solid (110 mg, 85%).CM6T-H.Pentachlorobenzaldehyde (100 mg, 0.36 mmol) and 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene (650 mg, 3.9 mmol) were combined in a flame dried round bottom flask with a stir bar and sealed with a septum.The flask was evacuated and backfilled with nitrogen thrice, then cooled to 0 °C before triflic acid (0.5 mL) were added.The flask was allowed to warm to room temperature overnight, upon which deionized water (20 mL) were added.The formed light-grey precipitate was filtered, rinsed with water, and purified by flash column chromatography, first using 5:1 hexanes:ethyl acetate to elute all the trimethoxybenzene, then switching to 10:1 DCM:MeOH to elute the desired product as a white crystalline solid (188 mg, 88%).CM4T-H.Pentachlorobenzaldehyde (177 mg, 0.64 mmol), 1-chloro-3,5-dimethoxybenzene (722 mg, 4.2 mmol), scandium triflate (177 mg, 0.36 mmol), and nitromethane (0.6 mL) were combined in a flask, sealed with a septum and sparged with argon for 5 minutes.The mixture was heated to 100 °C for 16 h, after which the brown solution was removed from heat and allowed to cool to room temperature before pouring into a separatory funnel with water (50 mL) and DCM (50 mL).The organic phase was separated and the aqueous phase was extracted again with DCM (2 × 50 mL), upon which the combined organic extracts were dried with sodium sulfate, filtered, and concentrated to afford a yellow-brown solid.This solid was purified with silica flash column chromatography (30:1 hexanes:ethyl acetate eluent), affording white crystalline CM4T-H (112 mg, 30%). 1 H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 6.61 (s, 1 H), 6.53−6.51(m, 3 H), 6.30 (m, 1 H), 3.80 (s, 3 H), 3.65−3.47(m, 9 H).HRMS (ESI) m/z: [M + Na] + calcd.for C23H17O4Cl7Na 624.8839; found 624.8854 (-2.4 ppm).A major side product (76 mg), eluting after the desired product, was identified via Xray crystallography as its regioisomer CM4T-H' with two chlorines in the ortho positions of the rings (see Figure S22).

CM6T + ClO4 -.CM6T-H (50 mg, 0.084 mmol), glacial acetic acid (1 mL) and a stir bar were placed in a round bottom flask and stirred at room temperature.In a separate vial, ceric ammonium nitrate (NH4)2Ce(NO3)6 (135 mg, 0.25 mmol) was dissolved in methanol (2 mL) and this solution was added dropwise to the acetic acid solution.The initial greenish mixture turns intense blue after ~1 min signifying the formation of carbocation.After about 15 minutes, when TLC showed the full consumption of starting material, the reaction mixture was poured into a separatory funnel with a saturated aqueous solution of sodium perchlorate (20 mL) and DCM (50 mL).The DCM was collected, then the aqueous phase was extracted twice more with DCM (2 × 50 mL).The combined organic extracts were washed with fresh portions of the aqueous solution of sodium perchlorate (3 × 20 mL), then dried with sodium sulfate, filtered, and concentrated to afford a blue solid.This was further purified by flash column chromatography on silica using a DCM:MeOH gradient (40:1 to 20:1) to afford the product (46 mg, 77%).NMT + BF4 -.Adapted from literature procedure. 5,11An oven-dried, three-necked round-bottom flask was equipped with a stir bar and a reflux condenser, charged with 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene (8.60 g, 51.1 mmol), and sealed with a rubber septum before evacuating and backfilling with nitrogen thrice.The flask was placed in an ice bath and dry toluene (50 mL) was added to the flask.n-Butyllithium (19.2 mL, 2.5 M in hexanes, 48.0 mmol) was added dropwise followed by N,N,N',N'-tetramethylethylenediamine (0.25 mL), upon which the flask was left to stir at 0 °C.After 4 hours, a solution of diphenyl carbonate (3.36 g, 15.7 mmol) in dry toluene (50 mL) was added dropwise.The flask was heated to 100 °C for 16 h, upon which it was allowed to cool to room temperature.The crude mixture was poured into a separatory funnel and washed with water (3 × 50 mL), then the organic phase was separate and poured into hexanes at −30 and left to sit for 20 minutes, upon which it was filtered to afford white crystals of corresponding triarylcarbinol (5.61 g, 67%).The crystals were placed in an Erlenmeyer flask, partially dissolved in approximately 80 mL ethanol, then HBF4 (12 mL, aq, 48 w/w%) were added.The flask was swirled vigorously for 5 min, diethyl ether (500 mL) was added and the flask was cooled to 0 °C for 30 minutes.The suspension was filtered to afford blue-black crystals of pure product (5.99 g, 64%). 1 H NMR (400 MHz, CDCl3) δ 6.05 (s, 6 H), 3.99 (s, 9 H), 3.59 (s, 18 H).Spectrum matches that reported in literature. 5CM3T.CM3T-H (70 mg, 0.103 mmol) and sodium hydride (38 mg, 60% dispersion in mineral oil, ~1 mmol) were placed in a flame-dried round bottom flask with a stir bar, which was then sealed with a septum.The flask was evacuated and purged with nitrogen thrice, then dry DMF (2.8 mL) was added.The reaction mixture was stirred at 50 °C for 24 h, then allowed to cool to room temperature.The crude reaction mixture was diluted with dry DMF (2 mL), and filtered from inorganic material, washing with additional portions of dry DMF (2 × 1 mL).The collected filtrates were concentrated in vacuo and the red crude solid was purified in the dark by silica chromatography using a 3:1 mixture of hexanes:DCM, affording a red solid that was further purified by HPLC with C18 column and acetonitrile eluent (38 mg, 54%).HRMS (ESI) m/z: [M] + calcd.for C22H11O3Cl10 672.7588; found: 672.7589 (0.2 ppm).Safety note: caution should be used in the filtration of the crude reaction mixture as sodium hydride exposed to air without a coating of mineral oil can spontaneously ignite.

CM2T.CM2T-H (70 mg, 0.102 mmol) and sodium hydride (38 mg, 60% dispersion in mineral oil) were placed in a flame dried round bottom flask with a stir bar, which was then sealed with a septum.The flask was evacuated and purged with nitrogen thrice, upon which dry DMF (2 mL) were added.The flask was placed in an oil bath at 50 °C for 16 h, then allowed to cool to room temperature.The crude reaction mixture was diluted with dry DMF (2 mL), and filtered from inorganic material, washing with additional portions of dry DMF (2 × 1 mL).The collected filtrates were concentrated in vacuo and the red crude solid was purified in the dark by silica chromatography using a 4:1 mixture of hexanes:DCM, affording a red solid that was further purified by HPLC with C18 column and acetonitrile eluent (55 mg, 78%), HRMS (APCI) m/z: [M] + calcd.for C21H8O2Cl11 676.7104; found: 676.7107 (0.5 ppm).Safety note: caution should be used in the filtration of the crude reaction mixture as sodium hydride exposed to air without the protection of mineral oil can spontaneously ignite.
DFT calculations

Figure S1.Correlation (slope defined as m) of the experimentally (CV) determined SOMO level of various trityl radicals with the SOMO and ionization potential (IP) calculated by various computational methods (gas phase calculations, 6-31G(d) basis set; CCSD, MP2 and HF energies were calculated on B3LYPoptimized geometries).The half filled points on the plot correspond to Me3HMT (-4.1 eV, CV measured on Me3HMT ClO4) 3 and Pyrr3HMT (-3.3 eV, CV measured on Pyrr3HMT BF4, see Figure S3), structures shown below in Figure S3.Ionization potentials were calculated as an energy difference between the relaxed neutral radical and corresponding cation, using polarized continuum model (SMD: DCM).Calculated with GD3BJ dispersion correction.*There was no minimum for the CM2T peroxy radical structure so the C-O bond was frozen at 1.6845 Å.As the ortho position becomes less hindered (H < OMe < Cl), the formation of the peroxy radical and peroxide dimer becomes more favourable.4.29 0.9 -0.9 Calculated using σpara = -0.27for methoxy and σpara = 0.23, σmeta = 0.37 for chlorine. 12S16 5. Additional UV-Vis spectra and photophysical data Figure S9.UV-vis absorbance of NMT + BF4 -, CM6T + ClO4 -and HMT + ClO4 -in acetonitrile; CM6T formed in situ in DCM after reduction of CM6T + ClO4 -with aqueous CrSO4. .Emission spectra of radical doped solid films (TTM@TTM-H, CM2T@CM2T-H, CM3T@CM3T-H) at low and high concentrations.The red shifts in emission with increasing concentration are likely due to self-absorption, the greater degree of self-absorption in CM2T versus CM3T is a result of greater spectral overlap between absorption and emission in the former.9.8×10 7 *This observed red shift in emission at high doping concentration is attributed to self-absorption.selfabsorption **The apparent decrease of kr in these conditions is most likely an artifact due to the larger margin of error for samples with low PLQY as well as pronounced self-absorption.The packing modes of CM3T and CM2T radicals are very similar, crystallizing in a P-1 space group with offset π-stacking between the methoxylated rings.This is in contrast to the packing of HMT, PTM, and TTM.The latter two compounds show offset π-stacking between the chlorinated rings, while HMT shows C-H•••O and C-H•••C short contacts with no π-stacking.TTM and PTM show large dihedral angles between the plane of the chlorinated ring and that of the central carbon (PTM: 46.1 and 55.4°; TTM: 47.0°).The DFT-calculated structural parameters of the radicals agree well with the crystal structure data, with the exception of PTM and HMT.PTM shows a dissymmetric structure, with two short (1.43 Å) C*-CAr bonds and one long.Interestingly, the crystal structure of HMT is also asymmetric, with one methoxy ring almost coplanar with the central carbon plane (12.9°) while the other two rings are highly twisted (58.5°).For HMT and PTM, the smaller dihedral angle is associated with a shorter C*-CAr bond as the conjugation between the aryl ring and radical centre increases.DFT calculations suggest that for both of these molecules, the crystal structure conformation is slightly less stable (PTM: ~2.3 kcal/mol, HMT: ~2.6 kcal/mol) than the symmetric conformation, so crystal packing may enforce these geometries (Table 1, SI-1).The rings in the CMTs showed twist angles between 45-55°, with smaller angles (~45°) between the central carbon and the methoxylated rings.The C*-CAr bonds for the methoxylated rings (~1.44 Å) are shorter than those for the perchlorinated rings (~1.47 Å), which correlate with increased spin density in the methoxylated ring according to DFT (Table S1).This could be explained by the donor-acceptor interactions between an electron-rich ring and the electron-deficient radical centre.
